title: Why the Moon has phases
description: Independent reconstruction of the official OpenMotionStudio reference. A real Three.js sphere, a fixed directional light and a moving observer explain the lunar cycle. Original procedural texture, English Piper narration and timed captions. No generated still images.
author: OpenMotion Studio · Equilibriumpress

scenes.name: Why the Moon has phases
scenes.headline: Why the Moon has phases
scenes.subheadline: One Moon, seen from a changing angle.

doodle.narration: Look up at the Moon over several nights and its shape seems to change. Some nights we see a thin crescent. Other nights we see a bright, almost complete circle. But the Moon itself has not changed shape.

scenes.name: Is it Earth's shadow?
scenes.headline: Is it Earth's shadow?
scenes.subheadline: A full Moon gives us a clue.

doodle.narration: A common explanation is that Earth's shadow falls across the Moon. That is not how ordinary phases work. Most of the time the Moon passes above or below Earth's shadow, and the Sun still shines on it.

scenes.name: Half of the Moon is lit
scenes.headline: Half of the Moon is lit

doodle.narration: Away from an eclipse, sunlight illuminates one hemisphere of the Moon. The opposite hemisphere faces away from the Sun. We see only the part of the lit hemisphere that faces us.

scenes.name: Change the viewing angle
scenes.headline: Change the viewing angle
scenes.subheadline: The light stays fixed. The observer moves.

doodle.narration: Watch the same sphere while our viewing angle changes. Near the dark side, we see a narrow lit crescent. From the side we see half of the visible disc. From the Sun's side we see a full Moon.

scenes.name: One orbit, four principal phases
scenes.headline: One orbit, four principal phases
scenes.subheadline: New Moon → first quarter → full Moon → last quarter.

doodle.narration: As the Moon travels around Earth, our view changes. At new Moon, the illuminated side faces away from us. At first quarter we see half the disc, then the full Moon. At last quarter the other half is visible before the cycle begins again.

scenes.name: A cycle of 29.5 days
scenes.headline: A cycle of 29.5 days
scenes.subheadline: The Moon moves eastward against the stars.

doodle.narration: The sequence takes about twenty-nine and a half days from one new Moon to the next. The Moon moves eastward by roughly twelve to thirteen degrees each day. On average, moonrise happens about fifty minutes later.

scenes.name: An eclipse is different
scenes.headline: An eclipse is different
scenes.subheadline: The three bodies must line up closely.

doodle.narration: During a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, and its shadow reaches the lunar surface. This only happens when the full Moon passes close enough to Earth's orbital plane.

scenes.name: Same Moon. New angle.
scenes.headline: Same Moon. New angle.
scenes.subheadline: The phase changes, not the shape.

doodle.narration: Next time you see a crescent, notice which edge is bright. The Sun is lighting a sphere, and you are looking at it from Earth. The geometry of sunlight and your viewpoint explains the changing shape.
